## Today

::: {.objectives}
1. Describe a trajectory with numbers: **step length, turning angle, speed,
   net displacement**
2. Why these numbers are **scale-dependent**
3. Random walks: BRW, CRW, Lévy — the null models
4. **Home range**: what it is, and what the estimators actually estimate
5. MCP, KDE and why autocorrelation broke them — **AKDE**
:::

# 1 · Describing a trajectory {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The step

Two consecutive fixes define a **step**.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Step length** $s_t = \lVert \mathbf{x}_{t+1} - \mathbf{x}_t \rVert$
- **Absolute direction** $\phi_t = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta y, \Delta x)$
- **Turning angle** $\theta_t = \phi_t - \phi_{t-1}$, wrapped to $(-\pi, \pi]$
- **Speed** $v_t = s_t / \Delta t$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.keyidea}
A turning angle needs **three** fixes. A step needs two. That is why
`filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)` exists.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

Turning angles are **circular** data: −179° and +179° are 2° apart, not 358°.
Never take an arithmetic mean of angles.

---

## Everything here is scale-dependent

::: {.incremental}
- Sample every 5 minutes: many short steps — but so short that GPS error
  randomises their *direction*
- Sample hourly: clear directional persistence
- Sample every 12 hours: few long steps, turning angles ≈ uniform
  (the animal looks like it moves at random)
- **Total path length** grows without bound as the interval shrinks — the
  coastline paradox
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
"Mean step length" is not a property of the animal. It is a property of the
animal **and your sampling interval**. Always report the interval alongside
it, and never compare step lengths measured at different rates.

There is a sweet spot: fine enough to resolve the behaviour, coarse enough
that a typical step is much longer than your GPS error.
:::

---

## Net squared displacement (NSD)

$$\text{NSD}(t) = \lVert \mathbf{x}_t - \mathbf{x}_0 \rVert^2$$

The squared distance from the starting point. A remarkably effective
diagnostic:

::: {.incremental}
- **Sedentary** — NSD rises then plateaus at a low value
- **Migratory** — a sigmoid up, a plateau, a sigmoid back down
- **Dispersal** — a single step up to a new plateau
- **Nomadic** — rises roughly linearly, no plateau
:::

. . .

Fitting these shapes as competing non-linear models (Bunnefeld et al. 2011) is
a cheap and surprisingly effective way to classify movement strategies.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
Two studies report mean step length for the same population of roe deer. Study
A reports 180 m, study B reports 640 m. Both are competent. What is the most
likely explanation?

- [ ] Study B's collars had worse GPS accuracy
- [x] Study B sampled at a longer interval
- [ ] Study B included migratory individuals
- [ ] One of them made an arithmetic error

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Step length scales with the sampling interval. An animal sampled hourly
produces shorter steps than the same animal sampled every four hours, because
the straight line between fixes cuts across all the wiggles in between.

This is why **step length is not comparable across studies** unless the
interval matches, and why you must state the interval in every methods
section.

It is also why Class 8's step selection functions always compare an observed
step with alternatives of *exactly the same duration*.
:::
:::

# 2 · Random walks as null models {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Three canonical walks

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Simple / BRW
Turning angles **uniform**; direction has no memory.

Diffusive: displacement grows as $\sqrt{t}$.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Correlated (CRW)
Turning angles **concentrated near 0**; direction persists.

Locally directed, diffusive at long range.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Lévy walk
Step lengths from a **heavy-tailed** distribution.

Rare very long steps; super-diffusive. Much argued over.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
These are **null models**. They tell you what a trajectory would look like if
the animal responded to nothing. Departures from them are where the biology
is.
:::

---

## Biased random walk

Add a preferred direction — towards a den, a water hole, a wintering ground —
and you have a **biased** random walk. Combine with persistence and you get
the BCRW, the workhorse null model for animals with both memory and a goal.

. . .

Class 8's integrated step selection analysis is, in effect, a biased
correlated random walk whose bias is estimated from environmental covariates.
Keep that connection in mind.

# 3 · Home range {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## What is a home range?

> "That area traversed by the individual in its normal activities of food
> gathering, mating and caring for young."
> — Burt (1943)

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Note what it **excludes**: exploratory forays, migration, dispersal
- Note what it does **not** say: nothing about a probability distribution,
  nothing about a percentage
- Powell & Mitchell (2012): a home range is a **cognitive map** the animal
  uses — and our estimators are crude proxies for it
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Every estimator answers a slightly different question. "95% home range" is
not a fact about the animal; it is a number produced by a method with
assumptions. Say which method, and why.
:::

---

## MCP — minimum convex polygon

The smallest convex polygon containing $x$% of the fixes.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**For**

- Trivial to compute and explain
- Comparable with a century of literature
- No smoothing parameter to argue about
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Against**

- **Convex** — includes land the animal never used (lakes, cliffs, cities)
- Extremely sensitive to outliers and to sample size
- Area grows with the number of fixes; no asymptote
- No density information — every point counts the same
:::
:::

. . .

Use it for comparability with old studies. Do not use it as your only estimate.

---

## KDE — kernel density estimation

Put a small "bump" (kernel) on each fix, sum them into a **utilisation
distribution** (UD), then draw the contour containing 95% of the volume.

::: {.incremental}
- Gives a **density**, not just a boundary — you can have disjoint core areas
- The answer is dominated by the **bandwidth** $h$
  - `href` (reference) — assumes bivariate normal; usually over-smooths
  - `hlscv` (least-squares cross-validation) — often fails to converge, or
    fragments the UD into confetti
  - `hpi` (plug-in) — generally the most reliable default
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Report your bandwidth selector. Two papers using "95% KDE" with different
bandwidths are not comparable.
:::

---

## The problem KDE has with tracking data

Classical KDE assumes fixes are **independent** samples from the UD.

. . .

GPS fixes an hour apart are nothing of the sort — the animal was 300 m away an
hour ago and will be 300 m away in an hour.

::: {.incremental}
- Effective sample size is far smaller than $n$
- So the UD is **under-estimated** — the home range comes out too small
- And collecting more fixes at a higher rate makes it **worse**, not better
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
This is why area estimates from the 1990s (a few dozen VHF fixes) and from
today (50,000 GPS fixes) are not comparable. It is not that the animals
changed.
:::

---

## AKDE — autocorrelated KDE

Fleming et al. (2015): first fit a **continuous-time movement model** to the
track, estimate the autocorrelation structure, and use it to derive the
*effective* sample size. Then do the kernel estimate.

::: {.incremental}
- Gives **confidence intervals** on the area — almost nothing else does
- Handles irregular sampling gracefully
- Tells you when your data are inadequate, instead of returning a
  confident-looking number
- `ctmm` package; also a point-and-click web app
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
If you report one home-range estimate in a modern paper, make it AKDE, and
report the confidence interval. If your CI spans an order of magnitude, that
is the honest answer.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You estimate a 95% KDE home range from hourly GPS data (n = 8,000) and get
12 km². A 1995 study of the same population using VHF (n = 60) reported
31 km². What is the most likely explanation?

- [ ] The population's range has genuinely shrunk by 60%
- [x] Autocorrelation in the GPS data biases classical KDE downwards
- [ ] The VHF study had larger location errors, inflating the area
- [ ] The two studies used different percentage contours

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Classical KDE assumes independent fixes. Hourly GPS locations are strongly
autocorrelated, so 8,000 fixes carry the information of perhaps a few hundred
independent ones — and the estimator systematically **under-estimates** the
range. The sparse VHF fixes, days apart, were much closer to independent.

Location error does inflate areas, but it is a far smaller effect than this.

The way to settle it is **AKDE**: fit the movement model, get the effective
sample size, and produce an area with a confidence interval. Very often the
modern estimate then agrees with the old one — and you have learned that the
population did not change, your method did.
:::
:::

---

## Choosing an estimator
| | Use when | Watch out for |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **MCP** | Comparing to historical literature | Convexity, outliers, no asymptote |
| **KDE** | Many roughly independent fixes | Bandwidth choice, autocorrelation |
| **AKDE** | Modern GPS data — the default | Needs enough data to fit the model |
| **LoCoH** | Hard boundaries (coast, cliffs) | Parameter choice |
| **dBBMM** | You care about the *path*, not the points | Assumes Brownian motion |

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
And before any of them: **should you be estimating a home range at all?**
For Leo the vulture the answer is no — not until you have segmented the track.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You compute a 100% MCP for an animal after 3 months, then again after 12
months. The area has tripled. What can you conclude?

- [ ] The animal expanded its home range over the year
- [x] Very little — MCP area grows with the number of fixes and has no asymptote
- [ ] The collar's accuracy degraded
- [ ] The 100% contour is invalid; use 95%

::: {.quiz-feedback}
The MCP is the convex hull of your points, so **every** new fix can only
enlarge it or leave it unchanged — never shrink it. Its area therefore
increases with sample size and duration without converging, which makes
comparisons across different tracking durations meaningless.

This is the single biggest problem with MCP, and it is why area-vs-sample-size
curves used to be standard practice.

Dropping to 95% removes the most extreme points and helps a little, but it
does not fix the underlying behaviour. A genuine expansion would need to be
demonstrated with an estimator that converges — AKDE, with confidence
intervals, on comparable time windows.
:::
:::

4. MCP, KDE and AKDE for one buffalo, compared
5. Demonstrate the autocorrelation problem by thinning your own data
:::

---

## Recap

::: {.incremental}
- Step length, turning angle and speed are **scale-dependent** — always report
  the interval
- Turning angles are circular data
- NSD is a cheap, powerful diagnostic of movement strategy
- Random walks are null models; biology lives in the departures
- MCP is comparable but crude; KDE is biased by autocorrelation; **AKDE**
  addresses it and gives you a CI
:::

. . .
